title: CQRS and event sourcing
scopeHtml: Scope: command/query split, event store, projections, snapshots, sagas, when not to use.

notes.title: Why separate reads and writes
notes.html:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) means using one model to change data (commands) and a different model to read it (queries). The idea comes from the observation that writes and reads have opposite needs.

Writes need validation, invariants and transactions on a normalised model. Reads need speed, joins pre-done, many shapes (a feed, a search page, a dashboard). Forcing one schema to serve both leads to slow joins, bloated entities and read load hurting writes.

Levels of CQRS, from light to heavy:

  1. Same DB, separate code paths (command handlers vs query handlers). Cheap and often enough.
  2. Same DB, read-optimised views/replicas (materialised views, read replica).
  3. Separate read store (Elasticsearch, Redis, denormalised Postgres table) updated asynchronously from the write side.

Worked example. E-commerce order page: read-to-write ratio 100:1. Writes: 500 orders/s into normalised Postgres. Reads: 50k order-status views/s served from a Redis/Elasticsearch denormalised document (order + items + shipping + customer name), one lookup instead of a 5-table join. The read store lags by 100 to 500 ms.

Industry examples. Amazon, Uber and Netflix use separate read models for feeds, search and tracking; Twitter's timeline is a read-optimised store updated by tweet events; Microsoft popularised the pattern in .NET (MediatR, Axon in Java).

Decision gravity. Level 1 is reversible and cheap. Level 3 is a major step: two stores, eventual consistency visible to users, projection code to maintain. It is hard to undo once clients rely on the read shape.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: the kitchen (write side) cares about recipes and correctness; the printed menu and the specials board (read side) are shaped for customers to scan quickly.

Common interview traps.

  • Using CQRS on a simple CRUD app. It adds cost with no benefit.
  • Not saying the read side is eventually consistent and how the UI copes.
  • Confusing CQRS with event sourcing (they are independent; see below).

notes.title: Commands, queries and consistency
notes.html:
A command asks for a change and can be rejected; a query returns data and changes nothing. Commands are named by intent (PlaceOrder, CancelBooking), not CRUD (UpdateOrder).

Mechanism: the command handler loads the aggregate, checks invariants, applies the change, and commits atomically with an event or outbox record. It returns only success/failure (and maybe an id), not read data. Queries hit the read model directly, with no domain logic.

Handling eventual consistency in the UI:

  • Return the new state from the command response (optimistic UI).
  • Read-your-writes: after a command, read from the write store or wait for the projection to reach the event's version (min_version token in the query).
  • Polling/WebSocket: show "processing" until the projection catches up.
data class PlaceOrder(val orderId: String, val userId: String, val items: List<Item>)
class PlaceOrderHandler(private val repo: OrderRepo) {
    fun handle(c: PlaceOrder): Long {          // returns version for read-your-writes
        require(c.items.isNotEmpty())
        val order = Order.create(c.orderId, c.userId, c.items)
        return repo.save(order)                // saves state + outbox in ONE transaction
    }
}

Worked example. After "Place order", the client calls GET /orders/{id}?minVersion=7. The query service checks the projection's applied version; if it is 6 it waits up to 500 ms then returns 202/retry. This hides a typical 100 ms projection lag.

Industry examples. Axon Framework, EventStoreDB, Marten (.NET), Kafka-based projections at Zalando and ING; Stripe's idempotent command-style APIs.

Decision gravity. Command naming and idempotency keys are cheap to design early and costly to rename across clients. Make commands idempotent (a client-supplied commandId) because messages are retried.

Everyday analogy. Dropping a request slip into a box (command) versus reading the notice board (query): the slip may be refused, the board never changes just by reading it.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning large read data from a command (couples the sides).
  • Non-idempotent commands retried by a queue, causing duplicates.

notes.title: Event sourcing: store the facts
notes.html:
Event sourcing stores every change as an immutable event; the current state is derived by replaying events. Instead of overwriting balance = 70, you keep Deposited 100, Withdrew 30.

Mechanism: an event store is an append-only log keyed by stream id (the aggregate, for example account-42) with a version number. To load an aggregate: read its events in order, apply each to rebuild state (apply(event)). To change it: validate the command against current state, append new events with optimistic concurrency (expectedVersion); if another writer appended first, the append fails and you retry. Events are named in past tense and never edited.

CREATE TABLE events (
  stream_id   TEXT   NOT NULL,
  version     INT    NOT NULL,
  type        TEXT   NOT NULL,
  data        JSONB  NOT NULL,
  occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version)      -- uniqueness enforces optimistic concurrency
);
INSERT INTO events (stream_id, version, type, data)
VALUES ('account-42', 3, 'Withdrew', '{"amount":30}');   -- fails if version 3 already exists

Worked example. Bank account with 1,000 events/year: rebuilding means reading 1,000 small rows (about 1 ms). A busy trading account with 5M events would take seconds, which is why snapshots exist (next section).

Industry examples. Banking ledgers and accounting systems (a ledger is event sourcing in disguise), Git (commits), Kafka as a log, EventStoreDB, Axon Server, Uber and Walmart for some order flows. Version-control and double-entry bookkeeping are the classic analogies.

Decision gravity. A genuine one-way door: the event log becomes the source of truth, event schemas live forever, and every query needs a projection. Only adopt it when you need audit, temporal queries or replayable history.

Everyday analogy. A bank passbook of every transaction, not just the balance; you can always recompute the balance and see how it got there.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing it gives performance for free. It adds work on reads (replay) and needs projections.
  • Editing past events to "fix" mistakes; instead append a compensating event.
  • Putting secrets/PII in immutable events (GDPR deletion becomes hard; use crypto-shredding).

notes.title: Projections and read models
notes.html:
A projection is code that listens to events and builds a read-friendly table, document or index. You can have many projections from the same events, each shaped for one screen.

Mechanism: a projector subscribes to the event stream from a stored checkpoint (offset/position), applies each event to the read store, and updates the checkpoint, ideally in the same transaction (or makes the update idempotent with ON CONFLICT). To change a projection: deploy new code, replay from event 0 into a new table, switch traffic, drop the old one. This is a main benefit: new read models can be built retroactively.

-- idempotent projection step
INSERT INTO order_summary (order_id, status, total) VALUES ($1,'PLACED',$2)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status, total = EXCLUDED.total;
UPDATE checkpoints SET position = $3 WHERE projector = 'order_summary';

Worked example. 200M events at 20k events/s replay speed: 200M / 20k = 10,000 s, about 2.8 hours to rebuild a projection. Parallelise by stream partitions (8 workers: about 20 minutes). Plan rebuild time into your release process.

Industry examples. Kafka Streams / ksqlDB materialised views, Debezium + Elasticsearch pipelines, Axon tracking event processors, LinkedIn's derived data systems.

Decision gravity. Projections are disposable and reversible; the event schema is not. Keep projection handlers idempotent and deterministic (no now() or external calls inside them, take time from the event).

Everyday analogy. The same diary read by a tax accountant, a doctor and a travel agent, each making a different summary sheet; losing a sheet is fine because you can rewrite it from the diary.

Common interview traps.

  • Non-idempotent projectors under at-least-once delivery.
  • Projectors calling external APIs (replay would resend emails).
  • Forgetting to monitor projection lag (latest_event_version - applied_version).

notes.title: Snapshots
notes.html:
A snapshot saves the aggregate state at version N so you replay only events after N. It is a cache of replay, not a source of truth.

Mechanism: after every K events (for example 100 to 1,000) or on a timer, serialise the aggregate state with its version into a snapshots table. Loading: read the latest snapshot, then events with version > N. Snapshots can be deleted and regenerated any time. If the aggregate code changes shape, ignore or rebuild old snapshots (store a snapshot schema version).

Worked example. An account with 1M events at 2 us each to apply = 2 s to rebuild. With snapshots every 1,000 events it reads at most 1,000 events, about 2 ms. Storage: snapshot 2 KB x 1,000 snapshots per 1M events = 2 MB, trivial.

Industry examples. Axon and EventStoreDB support snapshots; game servers and trading systems use periodic checkpoints; databases do the same with WAL checkpoints; Git packfiles are similar.

Decision gravity. Easy to add later, so do not add before measuring replay time; keep aggregates small (a stream should have hundreds to a few thousand events, not millions: split by time or lifecycle, for example one stream per month).

Everyday analogy. A bookmark in a long novel plus recap notes: resume from the bookmark instead of rereading from page one.

Common interview traps.

  • Snapshotting to fix an oversized aggregate; the real bug is the aggregate boundary.
  • Treating snapshots as authoritative.

notes.title: Event schema evolution
notes.html:
Events are forever, so their format must evolve without breaking old events. This is the hardest day-two problem of event sourcing.

Strategies:

  • Weak schema / additive changes only: add optional fields with defaults; never rename or remove.
  • Upcasting: a function converts old event versions to the current shape when read (OrderPlacedV1 -> V2), keeping stored data untouched.
  • New event type for new meaning (AddressChanged rather than redefining semantics).
  • Copy-and-transform migration: write a new stream/store with transformed events (heavy, last resort).
  • Use a schema registry (Avro, Protobuf) with compatibility rules (backward/forward) for the event bus.
{ "type": "OrderPlaced", "schemaVersion": 2,
  "data": { "orderId": "o1", "userId": "u9", "total": {"amount": 4999, "currency": "INR"} } }

Worked example. V1 stored total: 4999 (implicit rupees). V2 needs currency. Upcaster: if schemaVersion == 1 then total = {amount: total, currency: "INR"}. 200M old events remain untouched; new code sees only V2.

Industry examples. Confluent Schema Registry with Avro (LinkedIn, Uber), Axon upcasters, Greg Young's EventStore guidance on versioning.

Decision gravity. Event names and meanings become a public API. A bad event design (events that mirror table updates like RowUpdated) is a one-way mistake; model business facts (PaymentCaptured).

Everyday analogy. Old legal documents stay as written; a translator (upcaster) renders them in modern language when you read them.

Common interview traps.

  • "We'll just migrate the events" (rewriting history breaks audit guarantees).
  • Treating events as internal when other services consume them (they are a contract).

notes.title: Sagas and distributed transactions
notes.html:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services, with compensating actions if a step fails. It replaces distributed two-phase commit in event-driven systems.

Two styles:

  • Choreography: services react to each other's events, with no central coordinator. Simple for 2 to 3 steps, hard to follow beyond that.
  • Orchestration: a saga/process manager sends commands and tracks state (OrderSaga). Easier to reason about, one place for timeouts and retries.

Example order saga: OrderPlaced -> ReserveStock -> ChargePayment -> ShipOrder. If ChargePayment fails: ReleaseStock then CancelOrder. Compensation is a business undo, not a rollback (a refund is a new event).

Worked example. Saga timeouts: payment step times out after 30 s; saga retries 3 times with backoff, then compensates. Each step must be idempotent (a payment request key), because "timeout" may still have succeeded. Saga state stored as its own event stream, so crashes resume correctly.

Industry examples. Uber Cadence / Temporal workflows, AWS Step Functions, Camunda, Netflix Conductor; Booking and airline systems use compensations (cancel hotel if flight fails).

Decision gravity. Choosing orchestration (Temporal-like) over ad-hoc choreography is mostly reversible; choosing sagas over a single database transaction is a sign you already split services, so consider whether the split was right.

Everyday analogy. Booking a trip piece by piece: if the hotel is full after you booked the flight, you cancel the flight and get a refund.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting idempotency and the transactional outbox (writing state and publishing an event atomically).
  • Assuming compensation always possible (an email sent cannot be unsent).
  • Saying "2PC" for microservices without discussing blocking and availability costs.

notes.title: Outbox pattern and delivery guarantees
notes.html:
The transactional outbox makes "update my DB" and "publish an event" atomic without distributed transactions. The dual-write problem: if you save to the DB then publish to Kafka, a crash between them loses or duplicates the event.

Mechanism: in the same local DB transaction, write business rows and an outbox row. A relay (a poller, or CDC like Debezium reading the WAL) publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event id (a processed_events table or idempotent upserts).

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES ('o1','PLACED');
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload) VALUES (gen_random_uuid(),'o1','OrderPlaced','{"id":"o1"}');
COMMIT;

Worked example. 1,000 orders/s produce 1,000 outbox rows/s; the poller reads batches of 500 every 50 ms with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (multiple relays). Cleanup job deletes sent rows older than 1 day. End-to-end delay about 100 ms.

Industry examples. Debezium (Red Hat), used widely with Kafka; Shopify, Zalando and Uber describe outbox/CDC; event-sourced stores get this for free since the event store is the outbox.

Decision gravity. Cheap, reversible plumbing that prevents a whole class of data loss bugs; adopt whenever a service changes DB state and emits events.

Everyday analogy. Writing the letter and the "to post" note in the same notebook entry, so a postman can always find unsent letters afterwards.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual write without outbox, then claiming exactly-once.
  • Forgetting ordering per aggregate (key by aggregate id).

notes.title: When not to use CQRS and event sourcing
notes.html:
Most systems should not use them. They solve specific problems and charge a steady complexity tax.

Good fits: audit-critical domains (finance, ledgers, healthcare), complex domains with temporal questions ("what did the order look like on Tuesday?"), high read/write asymmetry needing different stores, systems that need many derived views or replay to fix bugs, collaborative editing.

Bad fits: simple CRUD admin tools, small teams without ops capacity, domains needing strong read-your-writes everywhere, ad-hoc reporting on current state (you need projections anyway), teams unfamiliar with eventual consistency.

Cost list: eventual consistency in UI, projection infra and lag monitoring, schema evolution, replay time, debugging with distributed logs, GDPR erasure complexity, steep learning curve.

Worked example. A startup with 200 writes/s and 2k reads/s: Postgres with an index and a Redis cache is enough. Adding event sourcing might triple development time with no user-visible gain. If compliance demands history, add an audit table or CDC to a log, which gives most of the audit benefit for 10% of the effort.

Industry examples. Many companies adopted event sourcing in a few services only (payments ledger, order lifecycle) and kept CRUD elsewhere; Greg Young and Martin Fowler both warn that CQRS is "a significant mental leap" and should be applied to parts of a system, not all.

Decision gravity. Applying it per bounded context is reversible-ish; applying it company-wide is the one-way mistake. Prefer a boring audit log until the pain is real.

Everyday analogy. Hiring a full accounting department for a lemonade stand.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending event sourcing as the default modern architecture.
  • Not offering the simpler alternatives (audit table, CDC, materialised view).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• CQRS = separate write model (commands, invariants) from read model (queries, denormalised); levels range from separate code paths to separate stores.
  • Reads in separate stores are eventually consistent: use returned state, version tokens or polling to manage the UI.
  • Event sourcing stores immutable past-tense events; state = replay; optimistic concurrency via (stream_id, version) uniqueness.
  • Projections build read models from events with checkpoints and idempotent handlers; rebuild by replay; monitor lag.
  • Snapshots shorten replay; they are caches, and a huge stream means a bad aggregate boundary.
  • Evolve events with additive changes and upcasters; events are a long-lived contract.
  • Sagas (orchestrated or choreographed) with compensations and idempotent steps replace distributed transactions; use the outbox/CDC to publish atomically.
  • Use CQRS/ES only where audit, history or asymmetric scale justify the cost; otherwise Postgres, replicas, cache and an audit table.

questions.promptHtml: What is CQRS and why would you separate the read model from the write model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know CQRS is about different needs of reads and writes, not a buzzword for "two databases".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CQRS means one model changes data (commands) and a different model serves reads (queries). Writes need validation, invariants and transactions on a normalised schema. Reads need speed and pre-joined shapes. When one schema serves both, you get slow joins and read load hurting writes. CQRS has levels: separate code paths on one DB, read replicas or materialised views, or a fully separate read store fed asynchronously. I start at the cheapest level.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Writes protect correctness: load an aggregate, check rules, save atomically. Reads want many shapes (feed, search, dashboard) and a 100:1 read:write ratio is common.

Level 1: same DB, command handlers vs query handlers
Level 2: same DB + read replica / materialised view
Level 3: Write DB -> events -> projector -> Read store (Redis / Elasticsearch)

Level 3 means the read side lags (typically 100-500 ms) and the UI must tolerate it. Example: 500 orders/s written to Postgres, 50k order-status views/s served from one denormalised document instead of a 5-table join.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking CQRS requires event sourcing (they are independent).
  • Jumping to level 3 when a read replica or an index would do.
  • Ignoring visible eventual consistency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is CQRS always two databases? -> No, level 1 is only separate code paths.
  2. What does the user see after a write? -> Possibly stale data; handle with returned state or version tokens.
  3. What is the cost of level 3? -> Two stores, projection code, lag monitoring, hard to undo once clients depend on the read shape.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "separate DB for reads". Senior: levels, the cost of each, and the decision gravity (level 1 reversible, level 3 not).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put a search index behind order pages cut p99 from seconds to tens of ms but then needed lag alerts after support saw "missing" orders.

questions.promptHtml: What is event sourcing, and how is the current state of an aggregate obtained?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know "store events, derive state" from those who think it is just logging.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Instead of overwriting balance = 70, I append immutable events like Deposited 100 and Withdrew 30 to an append-only event store keyed by stream id and version. To get current state I load the stream and apply each event in order. Changes validate the command against current state, then append new events with optimistic concurrency on the expected version. It gives audit and replay, but it adds replay cost and needs projections for queries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE events (
  stream_id TEXT NOT NULL, version INT NOT NULL,
  type TEXT NOT NULL, data JSONB NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version)   -- duplicate version = concurrent writer lost
);

The primary key gives optimistic concurrency: two writers both appending version 3 means one fails and retries. Mistakes are fixed by a compensating event, never by editing history. A ledger and Git are event sourcing in disguise.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing it improves performance by default.
  • Editing past events to fix errors.
  • Putting PII in immutable events (GDPR erasure; use crypto-shredding).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you query "all orders over 100"? -> Via a projection, not by scanning events.
  2. Two commands race on one aggregate? -> Unique (stream_id, version); loser reloads and retries.
  3. How do you delete a user's data? -> Encrypt PII per subject and delete the key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE describes the log. Senior covers optimistic concurrency, compensating events, projections for reads and the one-way-door nature of the choice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "edit the bad event in SQL" hotfix broke downstream projections and the audit trail; the fix was a compensating event.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce team added a read store (Elasticsearch) fed by a projector. Users now click "Place order", get redirected to "My orders", and the order is missing. Support gets 300 tickets/day, "my order disappeared", and some users order twice. Projection lag p50 = 150 ms, p99 = 2.5 s. The write DB shows the order. The CPU on the projector is 30%. Someone proposes "read from the write DB for everything".
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix the user-visible symptom without giving up the read store?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the projector faster" or "read from the write DB always". Faster helps but never reaches zero lag; reading from the write DB loses the point of CQRS.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens need immediate consistency (only "my orders" after a write)? Is lag a steady 150 ms or spiking (backlog)? Does the command return anything? Is the command idempotent against double clicks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return the created order in the command response and have the client render it optimistically; show a "processing" row.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) normal asynchronous lag hit by a redirect that is faster than the p99; (b) projector backlog under load; (c) projection errors silently dropped; (d) a stale cache layer.
  4. How I'd verify: compare latest_event_version - applied_version; check projector error logs and dead-letter counts; query ES for the missing id.
  5. Root cause: read-after-write on an eventually consistent store; the UI assumed strong consistency.
  6. Fix: command returns the aggregate version; client calls GET /orders?minVersion=7; the query service waits up to 500 ms for the projection to reach it, otherwise returns 202 and the client polls. Add an Idempotency-Key for the double order problem. Long-term: dashboard for projection lag with an alert at p99 > 1 s.
  7. Prevention: a test with an artificially delayed projector; lag metric in SLOs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not route all reads to the write DB (it kills the scale benefit); I would only read from it for the small "just written" window if the version wait is not acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Version wait exceeds 500 ms often? -> Return the optimistic state, poll with backoff, alert on lag.
  • Multiple projections lag differently? -> The token carries the version; each projection exposes its applied version.
  • Does the version token leak across users? -> It is just a number per aggregate; authorise the read as usual.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" this by adding a 2 s sleep after checkout. It worked until a Black Friday backlog pushed lag to 40 s; the version token approach would have degraded gracefully.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes faster hardware or reads everything from the primary.
  • Hire: identifies read-your-writes, proposes returning state or a version token.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency keys, lag SLOs, bounded waits and graceful degradation.

questions.promptHtml: How does a projection work, and what must be true of a projection handler?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Idempotency and rebuild are the heart of operating CQRS/ES.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A projector subscribes to the event stream from a stored checkpoint, applies each event to a read store and advances the checkpoint, ideally in the same transaction. Delivery is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent and deterministic: no now(), no external calls, time comes from the event. To change a projection I deploy new code and replay from event 0 into a new table, then swap. I monitor lag as latest event version minus applied version.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
INSERT INTO order_summary (order_id, status, total) VALUES ($1,'PLACED',$2)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status, total = EXCLUDED.total;
UPDATE checkpoints SET position = $3 WHERE projector = 'order_summary';

Rebuild math: 200M events at 20k/s = 10,000 s (2.8 h); 8 partitioned workers, about 20 minutes. Many projections can come from one log: summary table, search index, warehouse.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Non-idempotent handlers under redelivery (double counts).
  • Calling external APIs (a replay would resend emails).
  • No lag monitoring.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why same transaction for data and checkpoint? -> Avoids reapplying or skipping after a crash.
  2. Rebuild without downtime? -> Build a new table in parallel, catch up, swap the alias.
  3. Ordering across streams? -> Only per stream is guaranteed; projections must not assume global order.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes a consumer. Senior designs for replay time, idempotency, blue/green rebuilds and lag SLOs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A projector sending welcome emails re-sent 2M emails during a rebuild.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service uses event sourcing. Two parallel withdrawals of 80 on a balance of 100 both succeeded; the balance is -60. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void withdraw(String id, long amt) {
    List<Event> events = store.load(id);
    Wallet w = Wallet.replay(events);
    if (w.balance() < amt) throw new InsufficientFunds();
    store.append(id, List.of(new Withdrew(amt)));   // no expected version
}
fun withdraw(id: String, amt: Long) {
    val events = store.load(id)
    val w = Wallet.replay(events)
    if (w.balance() < amt) throw InsufficientFunds()
    store.append(id, listOf(Withdrew(amt)))   // no expected version
}

The table has version INT but only an index on stream_id, not a unique key.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and how do you fix it, including the retry path?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a synchronized block" or a lock in the JVM. It does not work across multiple service instances.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many instances? Does the store support conditional append? Is the command idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block withdrawals on negative balances with a DB check or temporarily route wallet writes through a single worker per account.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Both requests loaded version 5 and both appended; no unique constraint on (stream_id, version).
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT stream_id, version, count(*) ... HAVING count(*) > 1; replay logs.
  5. Root cause: check-then-act without optimistic concurrency.
  6. Fix: PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version) and append(id, expectedVersion, events); on conflict reload, re-check the balance, retry up to N times. Pass a commandId so a retried command is not applied twice.
  7. Prevention: a concurrent test firing 2 withdrawals; compensation event for the existing overdraft.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No in-process locks. Pessimistic locks work but reduce throughput on hot accounts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hot account with 500 writes/s? -> Conflicts spike; batch commands or serialise per stream via partitioned queue.
  • How to repair existing negative balances? -> Append compensating events, do not edit history.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team had the unique key but a retry loop re-ran the whole command without reloading, so conflicts kept failing; reload-and-revalidate is the key step.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: JVM lock.
  • Hire: expected-version append with unique key and retry.
  • Strong hire: idempotent commandId, hot stream strategy, compensating repair.

questions.contextHtml: A trading account aggregate has 1M events. Loading it for each command takes 2 s (2 us per event apply, plus read time). Command p99 SLO is 100 ms. A teammate says "add snapshots every 1,000 events". Another says "we will never need snapshots, just cache the aggregate in memory". A third notes the 1M events came from one account being used as a catch-all stream for all of a customer's activity over 4 years.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Redis cache" only, ignoring cache invalidation and instance restarts; or snapshots only, ignoring the oversized stream.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many commands/s on this aggregate? Do old events change behaviour? How often does the aggregate code change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Snapshot now: serialise state + version into a snapshots table; load snapshot then events with version > N. Tail of at most 1,000 events is about 2 ms.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the aggregate boundary is wrong (one stream per customer for 4 years); replay cost scales linearly.
  4. How I'd verify: measure load time vs event count; check how many invariants truly span the whole history.
  5. Root cause: unbounded stream.
  6. Fix: short term: snapshots every 1,000 events (2 KB x 1,000 snapshots = 2 MB, trivial) and an in-memory cache keyed by version. Long term: split streams by lifecycle (per month, per position) with an opening-balance event carrying state.
  7. Prevention: alert on stream length above, say, 5k events.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Snapshots are caches, never the source of truth; old snapshots are ignored when aggregate code changes shape.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Snapshot shape changes with a deploy? -> Version the snapshot; discard mismatches and rebuild.
  • Cache only? -> Cold starts and rolling deploys hit the 2 s path again.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team snapshotted aggressively and never fixed a 30M-event stream; the first snapshot rebuild after a bug took a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cache only.
  • Hire: snapshot + tail with numbers.
  • Strong hire: fixes the aggregate boundary and treats snapshots as disposable.

questions.contextHtml: An event-sourced order service has 200M stored OrderPlaced events. V1 stored total: 4999 (implicit rupees). Product now sells in USD and EUR, so total must carry a currency. Three consumers (billing, search, analytics) read the events from Kafka. A developer proposes a one-off SQL UPDATE over the event table at night. The release is in 2 weeks and downtime is not allowed.
questions.promptHtml: How do you introduce the new shape?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Migrate all events with a script": rewrites history, breaks audit and races with live writes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who consumes events and are they deployed independently? Is there a schema registry? Must old events stay byte-identical for audit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze the idea of rewriting; keep stored events untouched.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: upcaster at read time; new event version for new writes; copy-and-transform only if the old format must be dropped.
  4. How I'd verify: replay a sample through the upcaster and compare to expected V2; run schema registry compatibility check in CI.
  5. Root cause: events are a long-lived contract, and the first design implied a currency.
  6. Fix:
{ "type": "OrderPlaced", "schemaVersion": 2,
  "data": { "orderId": "o1", "total": {"amount": 4999, "currency": "INR"} } }

Upcaster: if schemaVersion == 1, set total = {amount: total, currency: "INR"}. Deploy consumers first (they accept V1 and V2), then switch producers to write V2. 7. Prevention: schema registry with backward/forward compatibility rules; events model business facts, not table rows. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No in-place update of 200M rows; no new meaning under an old event name.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Upcaster chain gets long (V1 to V5)? -> Compose small upcasters, or do a copy-and-transform into a new store when cost justifies it.
  • Consumer deploys late? -> Deploy order matters; additive and optional fields keep it safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team renamed a field and silently broke the analytics consumer for a week because nothing checked compatibility on the bus.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bulk update.
  • Hire: upcaster plus additive change.
  • Strong hire: deploy ordering, registry checks, avoids rewriting audit history.

questions.promptHtml: How do sagas replace distributed transactions, and how do you choose between choreography and orchestration?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand compensation, idempotency and why 2PC is avoided across services.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services; if a step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions, which are business-level undos like a refund, not a DB rollback. Choreography has services react to each other's events: fine for 2 or 3 steps, hard to follow beyond that. Orchestration uses a process manager (Temporal, Step Functions) that sends commands and owns timeouts and retries. Every step must be idempotent, because a timeout may still have succeeded.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
OrderPlaced -> ReserveStock -> ChargePayment -> ShipOrder
ChargePayment fails -> ReleaseStock -> CancelOrder

Saga state is persisted (often as its own event stream) so a crash resumes. Payment step: 30 s timeout, 3 retries with backoff, then compensate. Some steps cannot be compensated (an email); order them last or make them semantic ("apology") actions. 2PC blocks holders of locks if the coordinator dies and reduces availability, which is why it is avoided between services.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Non-idempotent steps retried after timeout (double charge).
  • Assuming compensation always exists.
  • Pure choreography for long flows: nobody knows the current state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if compensation fails? -> Retry with backoff, then alert a human / park in a dead-letter queue.
  2. How does a saga publish events reliably? -> Outbox/CDC.
  3. Isolation problem? -> Other transactions see intermediate states; use semantic locks or "pending" statuses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE draws a happy path. Senior covers timeouts, idempotency keys, uncompensable steps and saga state persistence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A choreographed refund flow with 7 services stalled silently; moving to an orchestrator gave one place to see stuck sagas.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders service: repo.save(order) then kafka.send(OrderPlaced). At 1,000 orders/s, a rolling deploy kills pods. Next day finance reports 1,400 orders in the DB with no shipment, and shipping reports 90 duplicate shipments. Kafka is healthy. Logs excerpt:

12:01:03 INFO  order o-88121 saved
12:01:03 WARN  SIGTERM received, shutting down
12:01:04 INFO  kafka producer closed

Another service shows ack timeout retries around the same time.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn on Kafka exactly-once" or "send before saving". The dual-write remains.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is publish inside the DB transaction? Are consumers idempotent? What is the partition key? Is CDC available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reconcile: query orders without shipment, republish with the same event id; consumers dedupe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) dual write crash gap loses events; (b) producer retry after ack timeout duplicates; (c) consumer not deduping.
  4. How I'd verify: diff order ids vs shipment ids; count event ids appearing twice on the topic.
  5. Root cause: two systems updated without atomicity; at-least-once delivery with non-idempotent consumer.
  6. Fix: transactional outbox:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES ('o1','PLACED');
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload) VALUES (gen_random_uuid(),'o1','OrderPlaced','{"id":"o1"}');
COMMIT;

A relay (Debezium reading the WAL, or a poller with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, batches of 500 every 50 ms) publishes; key by aggregate id for ordering. Consumers store processed event ids or use idempotent upserts. Cleanup sent rows after a day. 7. Prevention: chaos test killing pods mid-request; metric for outbox backlog age. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not claim exactly-once end to end; accept at-least-once plus idempotent consumers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Relay crash after publish before mark-sent? -> Duplicate publish; dedupe by id.
  • Outbox table hot? -> Partition by time, keep it small, CDC avoids polling.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added Kafka transactions and still lost events, because the DB write was outside them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "exactly-once" config.
  • Hire: outbox with consumer dedup.
  • Strong hire: ordering key, relay failure modes, backlog monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A 12-engineer startup runs an internal-tools SaaS: 200 writes/s, 2k reads/s, one Postgres, Redis cache. A new architect proposes event sourcing plus CQRS for "auditability and scale". The CTO asks you: yes or no? Compliance only requires "who changed what and when" for 3 account-setting tables. Nobody on the team has run Kafka in production. Page load p95 is 400 ms, with the slow query being a 5-table join.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend, and what questions do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agree because it is "modern", or refuse without alternatives.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exact audit questions must be answered? Are temporal queries ("state on Tuesday") needed? Expected growth 12 months out? Team's ops capacity? What is the slow-page budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the 5-table join: an index or materialised view; it addresses the p95 pain today.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the real needs are audit of 3 tables and one slow query, neither needs ES.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) the join; count audit query types.
  5. Root cause of the proposal: solving a problem the system does not have.
  6. Fix: an audit table (trigger or CDC to a log) for the 3 tables, a materialised view or read replica, Redis cache. Revisit CQRS at level 1-2 if reads dominate. If one domain (payments ledger) later needs history, event-source only that bounded context.
  7. Prevention: write a short ADR with the trigger conditions that would change the decision (read QPS, audit scope, team size).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not apply it company-wide; it triples dev effort and adds eventual consistency to the UI for no user-visible gain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Regulator later demands full history of invoices? -> Event-source or append-only ledger for that context only.
  • Reads grow 50x? -> Replicas, cache, then a separate read store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team event-sourced a CRUD admin tool, then spent two quarters on projection rebuild tooling nobody used.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: yes to everything or flat no.
  • Hire: cheaper alternatives with reasoning.
  • Strong hire: scoped to a bounded context, ADR with revisit triggers.

questions.contextHtml:
Order saga: ReserveStock -> ChargePayment -> ShipOrder. During a payment-provider brownout (p99 from 300 ms to 35 s), 4,200 customers were charged twice and 1,100 orders have stock reserved forever. Saga log:

ChargePayment sent  key=none
ChargePayment timeout after 30s -> retry 1
ChargePayment timeout after 30s -> retry 2
saga marked FAILED -> ReleaseStock sent
ReleaseStock failed: stock-svc 503

Provider later confirmed 3 of the charges had succeeded.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: causes and fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout" or "blame the provider".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider support idempotency keys? Is saga state durable? What retries exist at gateway and client layers too (retry multiplication)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause retries, reconcile charges against the provider's ledger, refund duplicates, release orphaned reservations via a sweeper.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: no idempotency key on the charge; timeout treated as failure although it may have succeeded; compensation not retried; retry storm worsening the brownout.
  4. How I'd verify: match saga ids to provider charge ids; count retries per order; check stock-svc 503 burst.
  5. Root cause: non-idempotent step plus "unknown outcome" treated as "failed"; compensation fire-and-forget.
  6. Fix: key = order id + step on every charge; on timeout query the provider for status before compensating; compensations retried with backoff until success, then dead-letter alert; circuit breaker and retry budget; saga timeouts persisted.
  7. Prevention: chaos test on provider latency, saga stuck-state dashboard, reservations expire by TTL.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: don't extend timeout to 60 s (ties up workers); don't use 2PC with a third party.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider has no idempotency support? -> Own ledger of attempts and reconcile via provider reports.
  • Compensation impossible (email sent)? -> Order irreversible steps last.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hotel booking flow double-reserved rooms until the team separated "unknown" from "failed" states.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tune timeouts.
  • Hire: idempotency keys and compensation retries.
  • Strong hire: unknown-state handling, reconciliation, retry budgets.

questions.contextHtml: Search projection over 200M events processes 20k events/s; live traffic adds 2k events/s. A bug shows wrong totals for refunded orders. You must rebuild the projection with no downtime. A junior suggests truncating the table and replaying. The projector also calls a tax API and sends a "refund processed" email.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Truncate and replay: users see an empty search for hours and emails resend.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is projection output served via an alias? Are handlers deterministic? How is partitioning done?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch the displayed total, or hide the field, while rebuilding.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: bug in the refund handler logic; event ordering; side effects inside the projector.
  4. How I'd verify: sample replay, diff to expected.
  5. Root cause: a handler bug, plus side effects mixed into the projector.
  6. Fix: math: 200M / 20k = 10,000 s (about 2.8 h); with 8 partitioned workers about 20 min, plus catch-up of the 2k/s live tail. Steps: fix code; remove email and tax API calls from the projector (move to a separate idempotent reactor); build order_summary_v2 from event 0 with its own checkpoint; run live tail in parallel; compare v1 vs v2 on a sample; atomically swap the read alias; drop v1 later.
  7. Prevention: replay test in CI on a fixed event set; keep handlers deterministic.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: no truncation in place; no now() in handlers (take time from the event).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rebuild too slow? -> More partitions, bulk writes, drop secondary indexes until finished.
  • Two versions disagree? -> Dual-run and diff before the swap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A replay re-sent a year of notification emails because the handler had a side effect.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: truncate and replay.
  • Hire: parallel build and swap.
  • Strong hire: math, side-effect extraction, diff validation, live tail.
